meta.title: aliro.mayday — your door key lives in your phone
meta.description: Open doors with your phone. The digital key lives in Apple Wallet, Google Wallet, and Samsung Wallet — no separate app needed. An access controller built on the open Aliro 1.0 standard.

hero.title: Your door key lives in your phone
hero.lede: No keychains, fobs, or plastic cards. The digital key lives in Apple Wallet, Google Wallet, or Samsung Wallet — right next to your boarding passes and payment cards.

1.title: Receive the key
1.text: The property owner sends you a digital key and your phone saves it to Wallet — just like a boarding pass. One tap, Face ID confirmation, done.

2.title: Tap the phone on the reader
2.text: No app to open. No codes or passwords. Face ID or fingerprint confirms it's you — and the key itself never leaves your phone's secure chip.

3.title: Door opens
3.text: Everything happens locally: phone and reader talk directly. No internet, no cloud — the lock works even when Wi-Fi is down.

why.title: Why this beats a dedicated app

1.title: Already on your phone
1.text: Wallet ships on every modern smartphone. No extra app to install, no account to create, no new password to remember.

2.title: Hardware-level security
2.text: The private key lives in a dedicated cryptographic chip inside your phone (Secure Element, Samsung Knox). It can't be copied even if the phone is stolen.

3.title: Works offline
3.text: Lock and phone communicate directly, with no server in the middle. Elevators, basements, network outages — all irrelevant.

4.title: One open standard
4.text: Aliro is an open standard from the Connectivity Standards Alliance (February 2026), backed by Apple, Google, Samsung, ASSA ABLOY, Aqara, and others. One key works with any certified lock.

migration.title: Gradual migration, no big-bang switch
migration.lede: You don't have to put your whole workforce on phones in one day. The controller reads existing cards from day one — your legacy fleet works alongside digital keys in the wallet. Employees migrate at whatever pace fits: one today, ten tomorrow, no "everyone at once".

1.title: Install the controller
1.text: The existing card fleet keeps working unchanged. Employees notice nothing — same cards, same doors, same ritual.

2.title: Import the card database
2.text: Card UIDs load into the controller as a single list (CSV / HTTP API). From that moment on, event log, card-to-employee mapping, lost-card alerts, and analytics turn on — same as for digital keys.

3.title: Migrate one at a time
3.text: An employee receives a digital key in Apple, Google, or Samsung Wallet whenever it suits them. The old card keeps working in parallel until you disable it yourself in the admin UI. No company-wide migration deadlines.

migration.formats: Supported formats: MIFARE Classic 1K/4K, MIFARE DESFire EV1/EV2/EV3, NTAG21x, ISO 14443A/B, FeliCa, HID Prox 125 kHz via external module.

standard.title: About the Aliro standard
standard.lede: Not a pilot and not a prototype. Aliro is the product of years of work by 220+ companies and two mature technologies — Apple HomeKey and CCC CarKey — merged into a single open standard.
standard.timeline_title: How the standard came to be

1.text: Inside the Connectivity Standards Alliance (CSA) — the non-profit IoT-manufacturer alliance — a working group starts on a unified access protocol, building on the proven Apple HomeKey and automotive CCC CarKey approaches.

2.text: On November 9, the CSA publicly announces Aliro. Around 200 member companies are already on board: Apple, Google, Samsung, ASSA ABLOY, Allegion, NXP, Infineon, and others. The stated goal — make the phone a universal key.

3.text: On February 26, Aliro 1.0 ships — a 195-page specification freely available from the CSA site. The ecosystem is now 220+ companies. The first certified locks begin rolling out.

1.title: Asymmetric cryptography
1.text: ECDSA on the P-256 curve for mutual authentication between phone and lock. The private key never leaves the phone's secure chip (Secure Element or Samsung Knox) — it can't be copied, even with device access.

2.title: Secure channel
2.text: AES-GCM with separate keys per direction and monotonic message counters. Any attempt to replay an older message or inject a forged one is rejected cryptographically.

3.title: NFC, BLE, and UWB
3.text: Tap at the reader (NFC), approach-and-wake (BLE), walk-through hands-free (BLE + UWB). UWB measures physical distance to the phone — relay attacks that forward signals from elsewhere don't work.

4.title: Cloud-free
4.text: Phone and lock communicate directly over ISO 7816 APDUs. No server in the loop — better privacy and no single point of failure: the internet can be down and the lock still opens.

standard.ecosystem_text: Apple · Google · Samsung · ASSA ABLOY · Allegion · Kastle Systems · Last Lock · Aqara · NXP · Infineon · Qualcomm · STMicroelectronics — plus 200+ more lock, chip, and smartphone manufacturers.

standard.disclaimer: aliro.mayday is built against the public Aliro 1.0 specification and is compatible with it. We are not a CSA-certified product — the CSA certification program is optional, paid, and not required to implement the standard. We do not use the "Works with Aliro" mark and make no claim to it, but the protocol implementation, APDU commands, cryptography, and the Matter DoorLock cluster integration follow the spec exactly.

integrations.title: More than a reader — it's a controller
integrations.lede: Built into your infrastructure: Telegram alerts, camera recordings on every access event, analytics, and remote control via API and MQTT.

1.title: Remote control
1.text: Lock and unlock from a Telegram bot, a Mini App, or through the HTTP API. Works from anywhere in the world.

2.title: Real-time alerts
2.text: Who opened the door and when, denied attempts, key-probing tries — everything arrives in Telegram at the right priority.

3.title: Video surveillance
3.text: Triggers camera recording on every access event. Frigate, UniFi Protect, Hikvision, Dahua, any NVR with webhooks, or via Home Assistant.

4.title: Attack detection
4.text: Detects replay attempts, NFC relay attacks, and case tampering — with a critical-severity alert in real time.

5.title: Analytics and metrics
5.text: Prometheus metrics, ready-made Grafana dashboards, a full event log. See who enters most often, when load peaks, where latency spikes.

6.title: Your own ecosystem
6.text: MQTT for home automation, Matter for Apple Home / Google Home / SmartThings, HTTP API for your own scripts and integrations.

roadmap.title: Work plan
roadmap.lede: Seven steps from hardware to a production-ready controller. Timings are approximate — broad strokes, April through October 2026, about six months total.

1.title: Hardware and platform
1.text: ESP32-S3 + PN532 rig validated, esp-matter skeleton builds and boots. Ready to move on to Aliro logic.

2.title: Matter + Aliro transaction
2.text: DoorLock cluster with the ALIRO feature — provisioning from Apple Home, Google Home, SmartThings. A crypto-verified NFC tap unlocks the door.

3.title: Real-device validation
3.text: iPhone tap via Apple Wallet and Samsung Fold 7 tap via Samsung Wallet. Both wallets must work against the same controller.

4.title: Control plane
4.text: HTTP API with a WebSocket event stream, a Telegram bot for alerts and commands, replay/relay-attack and case-tamper detection.

5.title: Integrations
5.text: Camera-recording triggers — Frigate, UniFi Protect, Home Assistant. Prometheus metrics, ready-made Grafana dashboards.

6.title: Backend bridge
6.text: The aliro-bridge Node.js service: hosts the Telegram bot, serves the Mini App for remote control, aggregates long-term analytics.

7.title: Production rollout
7.text: Security audit, OTA updates over Matter, field trials, tested behaviour on network loss and power-loss scenarios.

privacy.title: Your data
privacy.lede: The controller is built local-first. By default, nothing leaves your device. Any outbound integration happens only when you explicitly enable it.

1.title: The key never leaves your phone
1.text: The private cryptographic key lives inside your phone's secure chip (Apple Secure Element, Samsung Knox). Neither we nor the lock vendor have physical access to it.

2.title: No cloud accounts
2.text: No signup, no email binding, no payment card. Phone and lock talk directly — we have nowhere to register you in the first place.

3.title: Event log and alerts stay local
3.text: Who opened the door and when lives in the controller's own non-volatile memory. Suspicious attempts — replay, relay, key brute-force, card probing — are detected on-device and pushed to the owner through whichever channel you've enabled (Telegram, MQTT, webhooks). Nothing leaves the device unless you turn that channel on.

4.title: Verifiable architecture
4.text: The Aliro 1.0 protocol is open and documented in the 195-page CSA specification. The controller source is currently shared on request — for security audit and lab implementation; the public release is planned for October 2026 after field testing. Commercial use (selling devices, integration into paid products, OEM) is licensed separately — write to aliro.mayday@ilia.ae.

1.q: Do I need internet to unlock the door?
1.a: No. Phone and lock communicate directly over NFC (or BLE + UWB in newer modes). No Wi-Fi, no 4G, no server in the loop. Internet is only needed for the initial key provisioning into your wallet and for remote features like the Telegram bot.

2.q: What if my phone is dead?
2.a: Apple Wallet Express Mode keeps the iPhone responsive to the lock for about 5 hours after the battery dies — same as a transit card. Samsung has a similar Power Reserve. If the battery is fully drained, the owner usually has a backup path: physical key, PIN pad, or a trusted neighbour / concierge.

3.q: I lost my phone — can someone open my door?
3.a: No. The key requires biometrics (Face ID or fingerprint) before it will release a signature. Even if the SIM is removed and the phone is unlocked by passcode, Wallet still won't hand over the key without your face or finger. And if you revoke the key via Find My / Google Find or remove it from Wallet on a new device, the lock will refuse it on the next tap.

4.a: Any lock certified to the Aliro 1.0 standard — the list of vendors grows monthly (ASSA ABLOY, Allegion, Aqara, Kastle, Last Lock). Or our own controller on ESP32 + PN532 — you can build it yourself or buy a finished unit once available.

5.q: Can someone intercept the NFC signal and open the lock?
5.a: Classic replay attacks (record and replay later) and relay attacks (forward the signal over distance) are blocked cryptographically: every transaction is signed with a fresh, one-time keypair. On top of that, UWB measures the phone's physical distance, and our controller flags latency anomalies as alerts.

6.a: For yourself at home — yes, freely. Hardware is straightforward: ESP32-S3 DevKitC (~$10) + PN532 module (~$5) + a relay or electromechanical lock. Source is currently shared on request for audit and assembly; public release is October 2026, after which you'll be able to clone, build, study, audit, and submit pull requests. If you later want to sell devices based on it or deploy commercially — that's commercial use and terms are at aliro.mayday@ilia.ae.

7.a: Yes, under a paid commercial licence. Selling devices, deploying in offices / hotels / commercial buildings, integrating into a paid product, white-label, OEM — all on the table. Pricing is typically per-device, revenue-share, or a flat licence fee, depending on volume and scenario. Write to aliro.mayday@ilia.ae or reach out via ilia.ae to discuss terms.

8.q: If Wi-Fi goes down — does Matter / Telegram break, does the lock stop opening?
8.a: No. NFC unlock does not depend on Wi-Fi, Matter, or any cloud. This is an intentional design choice. Only the remote features (analytics, Telegram push, Home Assistant scenes) pause — they reconnect automatically the moment the network comes back.

privacy_page.title: Privacy policy
privacy_page.subtitle: Version of April 28, 2026
privacy_page.lede: Short, no legal noise. The aliro.mayday.software site is built to collect a minimum from visitors — ideally zero.

data.title: What data we collect
data.body: Nothing automatic. The site does not load analytics, advertising pixels, or external trackers. There is no cookie banner because there are no cookies.

local.title: What is stored locally in your browser
local.body: Only two settings in localStorage: the chosen theme (light/dark) and language (RU/EN). This data never leaves your device and exists solely so the page renders the same way on your next visit. You can clear it via browser settings at any time.

email.title: Email and inquiries
email.body: If you write to aliro.mayday@ilia.ae we see your address and message. We use this data only to reply to your inquiry. We do not share with third parties, do not subscribe you to mailings, do not add you to marketing databases.

third_parties.title: Third parties
third_parties.body: The site is hosted on Cloudflare Workers — Cloudflare sees technical request data (IP, User-Agent) at the network level like any CDN. Their policy applies separately. Beyond that, no other third-party services are loaded on the site.

controller.title: The controller itself
controller.body: The aliro.mayday controller operates locally and does not send any access-event data anywhere by default. Any integration (MQTT, Telegram, webhooks) is enabled by the owner explicitly — details in the "Your data" section on the homepage.
